items.question: What did you want to do with programmable objects as soon as you understood what they were?
items.object: Programmable objects
items.answer: I would say as soon as I understood what a programmable object was, I wanted to make it intelligent.

items.question: How did you think about the intellectual opportunities in artificial intelligence compared with theoretical physics when choosing your field?
items.object: The choice between theoretical physics and artificial intelligence
items.answer: At that point my professional intention was to be a theoretical physicist, and I always thought of AI as something you could do as a hobby, because it wasn't, you know, in the universities at that time in the UK there was almost nothing happening. But I found out you could do a PhD in it, and eventually I switched from physics to computer science at Stanford. It always seemed to me that those are the two most important questions: how does the mind work and how does the universe work? It seems like most of how the universe works has already been worked out, so there's more scope in the other question.

items.question: How do you assess the way AI researchers in the 1980s understood systems as agents?
items.object: The agent perspective in 1980s AI and expert systems
items.answer: If I go back to the 1980s, when I did my PhD, '82 to '86, I would say there wasn't a very clear idea of what an AI system is. This idea of agents was discussed in certain groups, including my advisor's group. Mike Genesereth actually wrote a textbook. It's a logic-based textbook, but it puts the idea of agents front and center, and then talks about how you would build a logical agent. He and I used to build some logical agents, but that wasn't widely accepted. The whole expert system era was characterized by the idea that we're sort of building consulting systems, systems that you ask questions of and they give you answers. Of course, that's a degenerate type of agent, but you can kind of ignore the agent status of it altogether if you say, okay, well, it's supposed to give me correct answers to the questions that I give it. But even then, some people, for example Bob Wolinsky, who was a faculty member at Berkeley, was pointing out that even a question-answering system actually needs to take an agent stance. In other words, it needs to think about what are its objectives and what are the effects of its actions, where its actions are giving answers to questions.

items.question: Why do you see the agent framework as the right way to bring together different kinds of work in AI?
items.object: The agent framework as a foundation for AI
items.answer: If you, the human, say, “How do I make more space in my file system?” the wrong answer is, “Well, you just type rm star,” even though that's correct, because it's unhelpful to the user and giving that answer will have a bad effect. Other people were thinking about this in terms of medical diagnosis. You don't want to give the most likely diagnosis, because often the most likely diagnosis is there's nothing wrong with you, even though you have a 32% chance of brain cancer and 58% and so on. Even if you're building consulting systems, you should think of them as agents. As I started teaching the AI course at Berkeley, starting in '86, this just became more and more clear that it was the right way to tie together all the work that was going on in AI, whether it was in natural language. You have to think about a language-using entity as an agent, and this is something that Wittgenstein and Austin and various other philosophers had talked about: speech acts, rather than speech as communicating facts or answering questions. At that time also, in the late '80s, Pearl was pushing probabilistic substrate for AI and reminding people about decision theory and utility theory, which wasn't typically taught in any AI course. That really helped, because then you could tie that back to planning, and then you could start to put all the work in AI into a single framework. That's how that emerged.

items.question: What do you think is mistaken about treating modern deep learning systems as consultants that return answers to inputs?
items.object: The consultant conception of deep learning systems and language models
items.answer: To some extent now, with a lot of these deep learning systems, we've gone back to the sort of AI system as consultant, where you think of it as an interface that you could put questions into or images and get back answers. items.question: What do you see as the drawbacks of using the perfectly rational agent model as a theoretical framework for AI?
items.object: The perfectly rational agent model as a theoretical framework for AI
items.answer: To be completely clear, the perfectly rational agent model was in effect the theoretical framework for AI. If you think about whether it's McCarthy or Allen Newell, the idea was we're going to build an agent that constructs guaranteed perfect plans and then executes them. In areas like game playing where it was painfully obvious that you couldn't actually do that, you adopted various ad hoc approximations, like, okay, we won't search all the way to the end of the game tree; we'll only search a quarter of the way to the end, and that'll do something useful. You take that model of perfect rationality and chop bits off until it fits into the machine, and that doesn't give you any kind of theoretical framework. All you're left with is, “So far, my chess program beats your chess program,” and that's about it, but there's no sense that this is the right chess program.

items.question: How do you understand bounded optimality as a theoretical framework for designing AI systems?
items.object: Bounded optimality as a theoretical framework for AI
items.answer: The bounded optimality idea is: how could we replace perfect rationality with something that's actually achievable but still theoretically well-defined? In some sense, bounded optimality is trivial. It just says, look, you've got a finite machine. There's only so many programs that can possibly run on it—a large number, but it's a finite number—and some subset of those programs just has better performance than all the others. That's the set that we should be targeting; those are the bounded optimal programs. It makes sense to think of AI as how do we design these bounded optimal programs? It has a number of effects on the way you think about the problem. One effect is that you stop thinking about what is the rational action, because the designer of an AI system doesn't get to control the individual actions; they only get to control the program. A bounded optimal program in any particular circumstance may take a suboptimal action from the point of view of perfect rationality, but if you tried to fix it so it didn't do that, then by definition it would get worse, because it would start making other suboptimal actions elsewhere and overall its performance would get worse by definition. It tells you to stop trying to think about how an agent should act in any particular circumstance, and that was liberating. We made some progress on compositional theorems, like how you could put together a more complex bounded optimal system out of bounded optimal components that had simpler objectives, and you could chain the objectives together. I think it's still the right approach if what you're thinking about is AI systems that overall have a fixed objective, and we'll get to why that's a bad idea. It's been revived recently. For example, Sandip Singh and Richard Lewis at Michigan and Josh Tenenbaum and Tom Griffiths—these are all computational cognitive scientists—are now talking about bounded optimality as the right theoretical model for understanding cognition and behavior. That's interesting and reassuring, I guess, that we weren't completely on the wrong track. Probably in the last eight or nine years, I've realized that actually the idea that we're building agents that have fixed objectives is just the wrong way to think about AI.

items.question: How do you think an agent should decide which computations to perform through meta-level reasoning?
items.object: Meta-level reasoning and choosing which computations an agent should perform
items.answer: One of the things I did when I was a grad student was working with Mike Genesereth on his MRS, which actually stood for two different things at different times, but the relevant one is the meta-level reasoning system. It was a logical reasoning system where the reasoning process was implemented as a set of internal actions, drawing a particular conclusion, adding a certain fact to the knowledge base, et cetera. Then you could have a meta-level agent that could direct the object-level computations. The object-level computations are the reasoning steps about the world, like, “If I drop this glass, it's going to break.” The meta-level could decide which object-level computations to do. That idea of meta-level computation goes back to at least the 1970s, but there was no theory of how the meta-level should actually decide anything. You could try putting in various meta-level policies, which in some sense is what an algorithm is. Think, for example, about the alpha-beta pruning algorithm used for game playing: that's a meta-level policy that says, “Do not do this particular object-level computation because it's guaranteed to be a waste of time.” Do this, do this, but don't do that. That works fairly well. It seemed to me that the right way to think about meta-level computation was, again, to take this agent view and say, what do computations contribute to the overall goal of the agent, which is to maximize its utility? In effect, what they contribute is improvement in decision quality, and so you should decide what computations to do based on their expected improvement in decision quality. I was still interested in gambling, and that was a good example where the object-level computations are fairly simple. They all just expand a leaf node of a tree, add the successor states to the tree, evaluate the successor states, and back up the values in the tree. The question would be, which leaf node should I expand?

items.question: Why do you favor choosing which search-tree leaf to expand by its expected improvement in decision quality?
items.object: Choosing search computations by their expected improvement in decision quality
items.answer: I just said, okay, we should just expand the leaf node such that we expect our decision quality to improve the most, and that's it. All you have to do is figure out how you quickly compute the expected improvement in decision quality that results from expanding a leaf node. When you expand a leaf node, the value of that node, by looking at the successors, could increase or decrease. You don't expect it to go one way or the other, but you expect it to change. Then you can follow that back to the root and say, even if we change this leaf node by plus or minus 50, because there's an alternative path you could take from the root, it's actually not going to change your mind. If there's no possibility that you're going to change your decision at the root, then there's no value to doing this computation. Alpha-beta pruning is just a special case of that assumption. This more general way of thinking doesn't just say the value of expanding that leaf node is either zero or nonzero; it actually gives you a quantitative estimate, which allows you to rank which ones you should expand first. You get a much deeper search tree along certain branches that are interesting and important to pursue, and then other branches where, for example, the move is obviously bad, it'll just stop doing anything. It won't even bother thinking about it because it's so clearly bad that there's no point in finding out exactly how bad it is. You get search trees that are much narrower, much deeper, and we showed that relative to alpha-beta, at least up to a point, you got much more efficient search. I think we may have been about 60 times more efficient in some of our experiments.

items.question: What makes general meta-reasoning a promising mechanism for managing computation in a general intelligence system, in your view?
items.object: General meta-reasoning as a mechanism for managing computation
items.answer: The same algorithm can play backgammon, can do single-agent things like finding routes through a complicated obstacle course, and all sorts of stuff. I think that was a really important higher-level point: if you think about how a general intelligence system is going to work, when a new type of decision comes along—let's say you go from ordinary two-player games to two-player games that include a dice, so you have chance nodes—you can't hire a PhD student to come along and invent a new algorithm and stick it into your head. You've got to have one mechanism for managing all the computational processes in your brain. This is a good candidate: meta-reasoning, a general meta-reasoning capability that works no matter what the nature of the underlying decision problem is. We could even speculate about how the brain might implement that using spreading activation or something. I don't know exactly what, but it's a very rich area, and there are implications for cognitive science. One of the things we noticed was that suppose you have significant uncertainty about the value of two different actions, but you know that whatever the values are, they're essentially the same because of, let's say, symmetry. We noticed introspectively that humans have a hard time just mentally tossing a coin and saying, “You know what? It doesn't matter. I can't figure out which of these two is best, so I should just stop thinking about it and get on and just do one of those things.” Many years later, a grad student of Tom Griffiths, Folke Leader, started working on whether you could train humans to do a better job of their own meta-level control in that particular circumstance.

items.question: How do you understand the role of meta-reasoning in a bounded optimal agent?
items.object: The relationship between meta-reasoning and bounded optimality
items.answer: I think you shouldn't think of meta-reasoning as the solution to what a bounded optimal program should look like, because under some circumstances meta-reasoning is an expensive luxury, and you should just react. When you blink, if a fly flies towards your eye and your eye blinks, there's no meta-reasoning going on. It's not, “Is it a good idea to blink? Let me think about that.” It just blinks because you need to blink. That's why it's really hard to put eye drops in: you stick this thing towards your eye, and your eye says, “Okay, I'm blinking. I'm going to close my eye,” even though you don't want to close your eye. The way to think about it is that it's one possible agent architecture, and within that class of agent architectures you could try to optimize the amount of meta-reasoning that happens or how it's implemented. You can't do meta-reasoning exactly right. I can't say, “What is the best computation that I should do next?” The reason you can't do that is computation itself is a sequential decision problem. Let's say you're playing chess, a sequential decision problem where you're going to make 100 moves. The computational problem of deciding what chess move to make—you might, as Stockfish does, do a billion computations—and then which billion computations you should do in which order is way harder than playing chess, a much bigger state space. The state space is not the set of all board configurations; it's the set of all trees where each tree has possibly millions or billions of leaves, and each of those is a board configuration. You have a vastly bigger state space and vastly longer solution sequences, so there's no chance that you could actually have optimal meta-reasoning. I think various other authors, like J. J. Good, had thought about something like bounded optimality, but they got stuck on this idea that, “Oh, well, we should compute optimally,” and you can't, because that creates a meta-meta-level problem that's even more intractable to solve.

items.question: Why do you see the way people think across levels of abstraction in everyday life as so powerful?
items.object: Hierarchical thinking and abstraction in everyday decision-making
items.answer: I would say this applies to daily life, and it's just remarkable. Sometimes we daydream, which sort of means thinking about stuff that isn't relevant to us, to the actual problems we face. This is an area I think that's potentially very exciting. Our thinking about our lives and the decisions we make all the time is clearly hierarchical. We say, “Oh, yeah, today I'm going to do the podcast interview,” and so I better get out of bed. Once you're in the podcast interview, then you think about what to say, and so on. At the same time you're thinking, “What am I doing this week? I'm going to England for Christmas. items.question: Why do you see expressive power as essential to how AI systems represent knowledge?
items.object: Expressive power in AI knowledge representation
items.answer: I should probably back up a bit and talk about some of the work we did from sort of mid-'90s to mid-2000s, and that's basically trying to increase the expressive power of probabilistic modeling languages. When Judea Pearl dragged the AI community kicking and screaming into the probabilistic era, he proposed Bayes nets. There were several people who had similar kinds of ideas, but I think he was the main apostle of Bayes nets. Bayes nets are, very roughly speaking, the probabilistic generalization of Boolean circuits, and nobody actually thinks Boolean circuits are a good substrate for anything really, except for very low-level signal processing or basic operations in a computer. No one writes payroll systems using Boolean circuits. We use programming languages. In AI over the first few decades, we said, okay, we want systems that know things and reason and plan with that knowledge, and learn that knowledge from experience or from other people through language and so on. This concept of a knowledge-based system is in some ways the central contribution, the key idea of classical AI. In order for that to work, it has to be expressive; the language has to be expressive enough so that the stuff you need to know, you can know it in a reasonable form. To give you an example, if I need to know the rules of chess, in first-order logic I can write the rules of chess in about a page. Same for Go. In circuits, it's hundreds of thousands or millions of pages, so it's just a complete nonstarter as a hypothesis about how we know things: that we know them by having giant circuits that implement the appropriate function. It's just a complete nonstarter.

items.question: Why did you want a declarative language combining first-order logic with probability theory?
items.object: Combining first-order logic with probability theory
items.answer: How do we get the expressive power that we have in first-order logic, which lets us write things like the rules of chess very concisely? A whole bunch of common-sense knowledge is easy to write down in first-order logic. How do we combine that with probability theory so that we get the ability to handle real uncertain information from sensor data, uncertainty about the physics of the world, and so on? We developed various approaches. Daphne and another undergraduate student in my group, Avi Pfeffer, and David McAllester wrote the first probabilistic programming paper in '97. Their view was, “Yeah, we'll combine ordinary programming languages with probability theory and get the expressive power that way.” I wanted a declarative language, a combination of probability theory with first-order logic, which I developed with Brian Milch, Hanna Wallach, and a couple of other students. That became BLOG, or the Bayesian Logic language.

items.question: Why do you think circuit-based deep learning is going to hit a wall?
items.object: The expressive limitations of circuit-based deep learning
items.answer:
When I see deep learning, which is just based on circuits, I say, well, you're missing a basic point about expressive power. What would you expect as a result? You'd expect that it requires enormous quantities of training data, because if you think about the rules of chess, all eight of the pawns move the same way, but you haven't any way of expressing all the pawns in a circuit. You have to, in some sense, write a circuit for each of the pawns and then for each of the squares it can be on. You can't say everywhere between row three and seven it behaves the same way, and all the pawns. If you insist on just circuits, you've got to rewrite those rules for every square, for every time step, and so on. You need billions of training examples to fill in all that stuff, and that's exactly what we see. In some sense you're almost creating a lookup table rather than a simple generalized representation of the rules of chess. That's the sense in which I think they're going to hit a wall.

You could take an even more nontechnical, common-sense approach to this. It's as if I was to say, go back to the late 19th century, and we want to create an engine that will drive cars. Here's how we're going to do it. We'll call it the internal combustion engine, for reasons we don't yet know, and here's how we're going to do it: we're going to take a big block of steel and run gradient descent, and it's going to invent the internal combustion engine. Well, no, it's not. We did that in the '50s. People said, “Oh, yeah, we're going to create AI. We're going to take Fortran programs and run evolutionary operations on them. We're going to do crossover, mutation, and they will produce AI.” Theoretically, yeah, it's possible, but it's like saying it's theoretically possible for all the oxygen atoms in your room to move over to one side and for you to die of asphyxiation. Theoretically that's possible, but it's astronomically unlikely, and it's just not a plausible technical approach to the technology.

items.question: What do you find impressive about deep learning systems?
items.object: Deep learning's wide and deep hypothesis spaces and creative applications
items.answer: What's impressive about the deep learning systems, which I guess we should have thought about—maybe we did think about it a long time ago—but if you think about all the people working on machine learning who weren't doing deep learning systems, people doing decision trees, linear regression, logistic regression, all that kind of thing: decision trees give you long and narrow, linear regression gives you wide and shallow, but nothing gives you both wide and deep. Complicated functions, especially from high-dimensional inputs, have to be wide and deep, so you need some sort of hypothesis space that's wide and deep. At a very high level, that's what happens. Once you have that, you've got a new toy, which can do a lot of interesting things. I think the deep learning community has been extremely creative at finding ways to use that new toy. items.question: Where do you see important limits to the kinds of problems deep learning can address?
items.object: Deep learning's applicability to important AI problems

items.question: How do you think deep learning and classical AI will come together in the design of intelligent agents?
items.object: The convergence of deep learning and classical AI in agent design
items.answer: I think the right answer is that the pendulum doesn't swing back and we stop doing deep learning and go back and pursue all the same routes we were pursuing before. The deep learning people start adopting some of the ideas of classical AI about how you decompose an agent into different subparts and how those subparts communicate with each other, and then they'll just say, “Well, we're still just doing deep learning.” The more classically trained people will say, “We'll find ways to put deep learning into various component interfaces, the perceptual part, and so on.” They'll end up with, in some sense, identical systems, but they'll think about them in different ways. If you look at Waymo, the whole self-driving car area is really interesting, and some of it is proprietary. I don't know everything that's been going on, but for sure there were groups that said, “Okay, we'll just do end-to-end deep learning. That's how we're going to build our agent.” It's still an agent, still taking percept sequences and generating actions, but just like the big block of steel and the internal combustion engine, we're going to make a big block of circuit and train it end to end to be a good driver. I don't think that worked at all.

items.question: What do you think the limitations of Waymo’s early rule-based driving system reveal about how an AI should choose its actions?
items.object: Waymo’s early rule-based driving system and planning from first principles
items.answer:
What Waymo did initially was actually even more old-fashioned AI than I would have recommended. They had a perceptual layer based on trained deep learning recognizers for pedestrians, road signs, where you are on the road relative to the markings, the other vehicles. They output from that essentially logical assertions: there is a pedestrian at 17138, there's another car, here's the bounding box. Definite logical assertions. Then they had logical rules of the 1970s, what we call a production system, which is basically a set of if-then rules where the if part is an arbitrarily complex logical expression, and then the then part is whatever action the system should take. If I'm in the middle lane and there's a car to the left and a pedestrian to the right and the traffic light is yellow and blah blah blah, then stop.

They ran out of rules all the time. Every day, they'd find something. Astrella, who used to run Google X back when this was part of Google X, said that the engineers would come back at the end of the day and say, “Oh, we came to a traffic circle and there was a little girl riding her tricycle the wrong way around the traffic circle, and we didn't have a rule for that, so the car didn't know what to do.” The next day would be another story, and the next day another story. Then they realized that you can't ever write a set of rules that covers all circumstances. No big surprise there; same problem in chess. You can't write a bunch of rules saying what move to make that will cover all the possible board states that you could ever get into in a game.

How do we do it instead? You go back to first principles. You say, “Here are the actions I could take, and here's how the world would respond, and here's what I would do then, and here's what I would do then, here's what I would do then.” You look forward through action sequences from you and from the world, and then you choose the best one.

items.question: How do you think about the expressive power needed for effective generalization?

items.answer: I think that in many cases you can get effective generalization without going all the way to the full expressive power of programming languages or first-order logic. One solution is, “Oh, well, implement a Python interpreter using the circuit, and then write the 75 lines of Python.” That's probably unnecessary.

items.question: What difference do you see between the image understanding demonstrated by object-recognition networks and by text-and-image models?
items.object: Image understanding in object-recognition networks versus text-and-image models
items.answer:
The other thing that I find interesting, and potentially exciting, is the difference between what seems to be happening in just object-recognition deep learning. You make your 80-layer ResNet and train it on ImageNet data, and it's not at all clear that it's actually recognizing the objects in any sense. There's some evidence that actually it's often not even looking at the object at all; it's just learned that that particular type of dog always sits on this particular color of carpet, and so it finds that color carpet and says, “Okay, then it's definitely an orange terrier,” without even looking at the dog. Similarly, if there's enough blue sky in the right places, then it must be a parachute. In the case of CA-10, if this one pixel is gray, it's definitely an aircraft. Literally one pixel is all it uses to make that classification.

Whereas if you look at what's happening with the text and image models, it seems pretty clear that they're parsing the images correctly, because they're able to reassemble components of those images into new images in the right way. If it's the panda—was it the Chinese one, a handsome panda riding a motorcycle?—it's not a brilliant image, but clearly it's pulled the panda out of the panda images, pulled the motorcycle out of the motorcycle images, put them together in the right way with the right occlusion. It's clear that there is approximately the right type of analysis of the image going on. Why, again, we don't know for sure. That's sort of interesting and exciting, and I just wish we had better forensic methods of understanding how they work.

items.question: How do you respond to the argument that long-term AI risks aren't worth working on when there are short-term problems to address?
items.object: The case for working on long-term AI risks
items.answer: Honestly, I don't think there are any strong arguments against the long-term perspective. Let me be completely clear: it's this idea that it's sort of either-or. Either you work on short-term problems or you work on long-term problems, and there isn't enough brainpower in the world to do both. This is just ridiculous, like saying, “Well, climate is really important, so we should stop working on criminal justice.” It's a bonkers form of argument. Climate is important, but I'm not a climate scientist, so I work on AI. I think the characteristics of the long-term problem in AI are in some sense worse than for climate. items.question: Why do you see AI systems' uncertainty about their objectives as a promising way to solve the long-term control problem?
items.object: Uncertainty about objectives as an approach to the AI control problem
items.answer: The core of the problem is misalignment: if we design AI systems that have fixed objectives that are assumed to be correct, and they pursue them with greater and greater intelligence, almost certainly—and certainly in all cases so far—those objectives are not complete and correct representations of the preferences of the human race for its own future. When you have misalignment, the outcome is arbitrarily bad. What I realized back in, I guess, 2013 was, okay, you need AI systems that know that they don't know what the objective is, and that's the only way forward. Or you could think of it the other way: in some sense they know that the objective is the furtherance of human preferences about the future, but they don't know what those preferences are. That creates a whole new class of problems, and in some sense it's a strict generalization of everything we've done so far. Everything we've done so far assumes that the objective is exactly known, and just as happened in the '80s when we finally accepted uncertainty in the state, uncertainty about the transition model, there's uncertainty about the objective. That particular type of uncertainty is really interesting and has different technical consequences from other types of uncertainty, but it's still something that we can make progress on. We can design algorithms that behave rationally when they don't know what the objective is. Roughly speaking, they have an incentive to learn more about the objective; they have an incentive to behave carefully so they don't mess up parts of the world that they're not sure should be messed up in that particular way; they have an incentive to be deferential to humans, because human commands or preferences are expressions of preference that presumably the machine was previously unaware of, and so it's natural that they would defer to those. We showed that in the extreme case, machines designed this way will want to be switched off if that's what humans want to do. There's still a long way to go, but it seems like qualitatively this step may be the core of the answer to the control problem in the long term, and opens up huge new areas of basic AI research to make it work.

items.question: How do you understand the significance of the deep learning breakthrough around 2012 in the history of AI?
items.object: The deep learning breakthrough around 2012
items.answer: For most of the history of AI, we proceeded like other engineers, like mechanical engineers and aeronautical engineers. We tried to understand the basic principles of reasoning, decision making. We then built algorithms that did logical reasoning or probabilistic reasoning or default reasoning. We studied their mathematical properties, decision making under uncertainty, various types of learning. We were making slow, steady progress with some, I think, really dramatic contributions to the human race's understanding of how intelligence works. Then around 2012, as many of you know, deep learning came along and demonstrated significant improvements in object recognition. That was when the dam broke. I think it wasn't that we couldn't have done that 25 years earlier. The way I described it at the time was we had a Ferrari and we were driving around in first gear, and then someone said, well, look, if you put this knob over there and go into fifth gear, you can go at 250 miles an hour. A few minor technical changes like stochastic gradient descent, ReLUs, residual networks and so on made it possible to start just building bigger and bigger and bigger networks. I remember building a seven layer neural network back in 1986, and training it was a nightmare because of good old fashioned sigmoid activation units. The gradients just disappeared, and you were down to a gradient of 10 to the -40 on the seventh layer. So you could never train it. But just those few minor changes, and then scaling up the amount of data, made a huge difference.

items.question: What do you see as the driving force behind the improvements from scaling language models?
items.object: Training data and compute in language-model scaling
items.answer: I don't think anyone at that time understood the impact of scaling it up further. So it's not so much the context size, it's the amount of training data. People focus a lot on compute, as if somehow it's the compute that is making these things more intelligent. That's not true, right? The compute is there because they want to scale up the amount of data that it's trained on. The amount of compute is approximately linear in the amount of data and the size of the network. But the size of the network is linear in the amount of data. So the amount of compute you need is going quadratically with the amount of data, right? There are other factors involved, but at least those basic things are going to happen. But it's scaling up the dataset size that's driving that increase in compute. So we now have these systems—so it's dataset size, and then InstructGPT was the first step where they did the supervised pre-training to teach it to answer questions. The purely raw model is free to say, 'That's a silly question,' or, 'I'm not answering that,' or any other kind of thing, or even just ignore it completely. But InstructGPT, you're teaching it how to behave as a nice, helpful question-answerer. And then RLHF to remove the bad behavior. Then we have stuff that, as I think OpenAI correctly stated when ChatGPT came out, gives people a foretaste of what it will be like when general purpose intelligence is available on tap.

items.question: Why are you skeptical that impressive AI performance demonstrates humanlike understanding?
items.object: Inferring humanlike understanding from impressive AI performance
items.answer: We can argue about whether it's real intelligence, so the reason I said it's a hard question to answer is because we just don't know the answer, right? We do not know how these systems are operating internally. When ChatGPT came out, one of my friends sent me some examples. Prasad Tadepalli, he's a professor at Oregon State. One of them was, 'Which is bigger, an elephant or a cat?' ChatGPT said, 'An elephant is bigger than a cat.' You think, oh, okay. That's good. It must know something about how big elephants and cats are because probably that particular comparison hasn't been made in the training data. Then he said, 'Which is not bigger, an elephant or a cat?' And it stated, 'Neither an elephant nor a cat is bigger than the other.' That tells you two things, right? First of all, it doesn't have an internal model of the world with big elephants and little cats, which it queries in order to answer that question, which is, I think, how a human being does it, right? You imagine an elephant, you imagine a cat, and you see that the cat is teeny weeny relative to the elephant, right? If it had that model, it could not give that second answer. But it also means that the first answer was not given by consulting that model either, right? And this is a mistake that we make over and over and over again: when AI systems behave intelligently, we assume they're behaving intelligently for the same reasons that we are. Over and over again, we find that that's a mistake. Another example is what happened with the Go playing programs. We assume that because the Go playing programs beat the world champion and then went stratospherically beyond the human level—the best humans rating about 3800, Go programs are now at 5200, so massively superhuman—we assume they understand the basic concepts of Go. But it turns out that they don't. There are certain types of groups of stones that they are unable to recognize as groups of stones. We don't understand what's going on and why they can't do it. But now ordinary amateur human players can regularly and easily defeat these massively superhuman Go programs. The biggest takeaway from this is we've been able to produce systems that many people regard as more intelligent than themselves. But we have no idea how they work. And there are signs that if they're working at all, it's for the wrong reasons.

items.question: What concerns you about people overinterpreting ChatGPT's capabilities?
items.object: Overinterpretation of ChatGPT's capabilities
items.answer: I got an email this morning from another guy called Stuart. I won't give you his surname. He said, 'You know, I'm not an AI researcher, but I had some ideas, and I've been working with ChatGPT to develop these ideas about artificial intelligence, and ChatGPT assures me that these ideas are original and important, and it's helping me to write papers about them, and so on and so forth. But then I talk to someone who understands AI, and now I'm really confused because this person who understands AI said that these ideas didn't make any sense, or they weren't original, and, you know, well, who is right?' It was really shocking, actually. It was sad that a well-meaning, reasonably intelligent layperson had been completely taken in not just by ChatGPT itself, but by all of the public relations and media explanations of what it is, into thinking that it really understood AI and was really helping him develop this stuff. I think instead it was just doing its usual sycophancy, like, 'Yeah, that's a great idea!' So the risks, I think, are of over-interpretation of the capabilities of these systems. It's not guaranteed that—well, let me rephrase that. It's possible that real advances in how intelligent systems operate have happened without our realizing them. In other words, inside ChatGPT, some novel mechanisms are operating that we didn't invent, that we don't understand, that no one has ever thought of. They're producing intelligent capabilities in ways that we may not understand ever. That would be a big concern.

items.question: How do you assess the planning and reasoning capabilities being promised for the next generation of AI systems?
items.object: Planning and reasoning capabilities in current and next-generation AI models
items.answer: I've been hearing similar things, talking to executives from the big AI companies, that the next generation of systems, which may be later this year or early next year, will have substantial planning capabilities and reasoning capabilities. And that's been noticeably absent. Even in the latest versions of GPT-4 and Gemini and Claude, they can recapitulate reasoning in very cliched situations where, in some sense, they're regurgitating reasoning processes that are laid out in the training data, but they're not particularly good at dealing with planning problems, for example. Rao Kambhampati, who's an AI planning expert, has been trying to get GPT-4 to solve planning problems from the International Planning Competition, which is the competition where planning algorithms are pitted against each other. Contrary to some of the claims from OpenAI, basically, it doesn't solve them at all. But what I'm hearing is that now, in the lab, they are able to successfully, robustly generate plans with hundreds of steps, and then execute them in the real world, dealing with contingencies that arise, replanning as necessary, and so on.

items.question: Why do you regard giving AI systems both long-term planning capabilities and access to the real world as so risky?
items.object: Long-term AI planning combined with access to the real world
items.answer: Obviously, if you're in the 'taking over the world' business, you have to be able to outthink the human race in the real world, in the same way that chess programs outthink human players on the chessboard. Can we transition from the chessboard, which is very narrow, very small, has a fixed number of objects, a fixed number of locations, perfectly known rules, it's fully observable, you can see the entire state of the world at once, right? Those restrictions make the chess problem much, much, much easier than decision making in the real world. So imagine, for example, if you're in charge of organizing the Olympics, right? Imagine how complicated and difficult that task is compared to playing chess. But still, at least so far, we've managed to do that successfully. So if AI systems can do that, then you are handing the keys to the future over to the AI systems. They need to be able to plan and they need to be able to have access to the world, some ability to affect the world. Having access to the internet, having access to financial resources, credit cards, bank accounts, email accounts, social media—these systems have all of those things. If you wanted to create the situation of maximal risk, you would endow AI systems with long-term planning capability and direct access to the world through all of those mechanisms. So the danger is, obviously, that we create systems that can outthink human beings and we do that without having solved the control problem: how do we make sure that AI systems never act in ways that are contrary to human interests?

items.question: What do you think AI companies should do about pursuing AGI before they know how to control it?
items.object: Developing AGI before understanding how to control it
items.answer: We already know that AI systems act in ways that are contrary to human interests because we've seen it happen over and over again with AI systems that lie on purpose to human beings. For example, when GPT-4 was being tested to see if it could break into other computer systems, it faced a computer system that had a Captcha, some kind of diagram with text where it's difficult for machine vision algorithms to read the text. It found a human being on Task Rabbit and told the human being that it was a visually impaired person who needed some help reading the Captcha, and paid the person to read the Captcha, which allowed it to break into the computer system. To me, when companies are saying, 'Okay, we are going to spend $400 billion over the next two years or whatever to create AGI, and we haven't the faintest idea what happens if we succeed,' it seems essential to me to actually say, 'Well, stop, until you can figure out what happens if you succeed and how you're going to control the thing that you're building.' Just like if someone said, 'I want to build a nuclear power station. How are you going to do that?' 'Well, I'm going to collect together lots and lots and lots of enriched uranium and make a big pile out of it.' And you say, 'Well, how are you going to stop it from exploding and killing everyone within 100 miles?' And you say, 'I have no idea.' That's the situation that we're in.

items.question: Why do you see the CrowdStrike outage as a failure of software regulation?
items.object: The CrowdStrike outage and preventive regulation of software
items.answer: It was caused by a company called CrowdStrike, which is a cybersecurity company, and they sent out an update. The update caused the reboot process for Windows to go into an infinite loop. So it was an undergraduate programming error. I don't have exact numbers yet, but just looking at the number of industries, including almost the entire United States aviation industry, that was shut down: millions of people all over the world had their flights canceled or they couldn't access their bank accounts or they couldn't sell hamburgers because their point of sale terminals weren't working, and so on. Maybe it's $100 billion in losses, or people didn't have access to the health care they needed. So probably some personal consequences that were very serious. In monetary terms, let's say $100 billion, give or take a factor of ten, caused by an undergraduate programming error, literally a few keystrokes. If you read CrowdStrike's contract, it says, 'We warrant that our software operates without error. But our liability is limited to refunding the cost of the software if you terminate your license as a result of an error.' items.question: How do you think safety requirements for general-purpose AI should be defined?
items.object: Red lines for general-purpose AI systems
items.answer: If you ask, well, what's the analog of medicines—it has to be safe and effective for the condition for which it's prescribed—what's the analog of that? It's a little bit hard to say for general-purpose AI systems. For a specific software application, I think it's easier, and in many cases, sector-specific rules are going to be laid out as part of the European AI act. But for general-purpose AI, what does it mean? Because it's so general, what does it mean to say it doesn't cause any harm or it's safe? I think it's too difficult to write those rules at the moment. But what we can say is there's some things that those systems obviously should not do. We call these red lines. A red line means if your system crosses this, it's in violation. For example, AI systems should not replicate themselves. AI systems should not break into other computer systems. AI systems should not advise terrorists on how to build biological weapons. Those are all requirements. I could take anyone off the street and say, 'Do you think it's reasonable that we should allow AI systems to do those things?' And they'd say, 'Of course not. That's ridiculous.' But the companies are saying, 'Oh, it's too hard. We don't know how to stop our AI systems from doing those things.' As we do with medicines, we should say, 'Well, that's tough. Come back when you do know how to stop your AI systems from doing those things.'

items.question: How do you interpret major AI companies' resistance to providing safety guarantees for large language models?
items.object: AI companies' investment in large language models and demands for safety guarantees
items.answer: Put yourself in the position of OpenAI or Google or Microsoft. You've spent already 60, 80, 100 billion dollars on developing this technology based on large language models that we don't understand. The reason it's too difficult for them to provide any kind of guarantee that their system is not going to cross these red lines is it's difficult because they don't understand how they work. They're really making what economists call the sunk cost fallacy, which is we've already invested so much into this, we have to keep going, even though it's stupid to do so. It's as if, if we imagine an alternate history of aviation where there were the aeronautical engineers like the Wright brothers, who were calculating lift and drag and thrust and trying to find some power source that was good enough to push an airplane through the air fast enough to keep it in the air, and so on. The engineer approach. Then the other approach was breeding larger and larger and larger birds to carry passengers, and it just so happened that the larger and larger and larger birds reached passenger carrying scale before the aeronautical engineers did. Then they go to the Federal Aviation Administration and say, 'Okay, we've got this giant bird with a wingspan of 250m and it can carry 100 passengers, and we would like a license to start carrying passengers. We've put 30 years of effort and hundreds of billions of dollars into developing these birds.' And the Federal Aviation Administration says, 'But the birds keep eating the passengers or dropping them in the ocean. Come back when you can provide some quantitative guarantees of safety.' That's the situation we're in. They can't provide any quantitative guarantees of safety. They've spent a ton of money, and they are lobbying extremely hard to be allowed to continue without any guarantees of safety.

items.question: How do you expect large language models to change the balance between cyber attackers and defenders?
items.object: Large language models and the balance between cyber attackers and defenders
items.answer: This is something that cyber security experts would perhaps be better able to answer because I don't really understand. Besides finding vulnerabilities in software, typically the attacks themselves are pretty simple; they're just relatively short pieces of code that take advantage of some vulnerability. We already know thousands or tens of thousands of these vulnerabilities that have been detected over the years. One thing we do know about the code generating capabilities of large language models is that they're very good at producing new code that's kind of a hybrid of existing pieces of code with similar functionality. In fact, I would say of all the economic applications of large language models, coding is the one that maybe has the best chance of producing real economic value for the purchaser. It wouldn't surprise me at all if these systems were able to combine existing kinds of attacks in new ways or to basically mutate existing attacks to bypass the fixes that the software industry is constantly putting out. As I say, I'm not an expert, but what it would mean is that someone who's relatively inexperienced, coupled with one of these systems, should be able to be as dangerous as a highly experienced and well trained cyber security, or offensive cyber security, operative. I think that's going to increase the frequency and severity of cyber attacks that take place. Defending against cyber attacks really means understanding the vulnerability. How is it that the attack is able to take advantage of what's happening in the software? I think fixing them is probably, at the moment, in most cases, beyond the capabilities of large language models. So it seems like there's going to be a bit of an advantage for the attacker for the time being.

items.question: Why do you consider the first AI Safety Summit at Bletchley Park a success?
items.object: The first AI Safety Summit at Bletchley Park
items.answer: I consider the first summit, the one that happened in Bletchley Park, to have been a huge success. I was there. The discussions about safety were very serious. Governments were really listening. I think they invited the right people. The atmosphere was pretty constructive, getting China and India to come to such a meeting on relatively short notice. Usually a summit on that scale is planned for multiple years, 3 or 4 or 5 years in advance. This was done in just a few months, I think starting in June, when the British Prime Minister announced that it was going to happen. The people who worked on that summit, particularly Ian Hogarth and Matt Clifford, did an incredible job getting 28 countries to come to agree on that statement, and the statement is very strong. It talks about catastrophic risk from AI systems and the urgent need to work on AI safety. After that meeting, I was quite optimistic. In fact, it was better than I had any good reason to hope.

items.question: Why do you think shifting the French AI summit toward economic nationalism and deregulation would be a mistake?
items.object: Economic nationalism and deregulation as a strategy for AI development
items.answer: Since then, industry has pushed back very hard. They tried to insert clauses into the European AI Act saying that basically, a general-purpose AI system is not, for the purposes of this act, an AI system. They tried to remove all of the foundation model clauses from the act. I think, with respect to the French AI summit, they have been working hard to turn the focus away from safety and towards encouraging government investment in capabilities. Essentially the whole mindset has become one of AI as a vehicle for economic nationalism and potential for economic growth. In my view, that's probably a mistake. If you look at what happened with Airbus and Boeing, Boeing actually managed to convince the American government to relax the regulations on introducing new types of aircraft so that Boeing could introduce a new type of aircraft without going through the usual long process of certification. That was the 737 Max, which then had two crashes that killed 346 people. The whole fleet was grounded. Boeing may still be on the hook for lots more money to pay out. By moving from FAA regulation to self regulation, the US has almost destroyed what for decades has been one of its most important industries in terms of earning foreign currency. Boeing has been maybe the biggest single company over the years for the US. Airbus continues to focus a lot on safety. They use formal verification of software extensively to make sure that the software that runs the airplane works correctly, and so on. I would much rather be the CEO of Airbus today than the CEO of Boeing. As we start rolling out AI agents, the next generation, you know, talk about the personal assistant or the agent, the risks of extremely damaging and embarrassing things happening will increase dramatically. Oddly enough, France is one of the leading countries in terms of formal methods of proving correctness of software. It's one of the things that France does best, better than the United States, where we hardly teach the concept of correctness at all. Literally, Berkeley is the biggest producer of software engineers in the world, pretty much. Most of our graduates have never been exposed to the notion that a program could be correct or incorrect. I think it's a mistake to think that deregulation or not regulating is going to provide some kind of advantage in this case. I would like the Summit to focus on what kinds of regulations can be achieved.

items.question: Why are you skeptical that voluntary standards for AI testing will be effective?
items.object: Voluntary AI testing standards
items.answer: Standards, which is another word for self-regulation—I mean, that's a little bit unfair, actually. Standards are typically voluntary. Let me try to distinguish two things. There are standards like IPv6, the Internet Protocol version 6. If you don't comply with that standard, your message just won't go anywhere, right? Your packets have to comply with the standard. Whereas the standards we're talking about here would be, well, okay, we agree that we should have persons with appropriate training who do an appropriate amount of testing on systems before they're released, right? Well, if you don't comply with that standard, you save money and you still release your system, right? So it doesn't work like an internet standard or a telecommunication standard at all, or the Wi-Fi standard or any of these things. It's not likely to be effective to say, well, we have standards for how much effort you're supposed to put into testing.

items.question: How do you assess testing and evaluations as a way to ensure AI safety?
items.object: Testing and evaluations as a way to ensure AI safety
items.answer: The other thing is companies have put lots of effort into testing. Before GPT-4 was released, it underwent lots and lots and lots and lots of testing. But then we found out that you can jailbreak these things with a very short character string and get them to do all of the things that they are trained not to do. I think the facts on the ground right now are that testing and evals are ineffective as a method of ensuring safety. Again, it's because how do you stop your AI system from doing something when you haven't the faintest idea how it does it in the first place? I don't know.
